title: Profiling-driven kernel specialization and dynamic launch adaptor
body:
Goal: sketch an approach for using lightweight production profiling to choose per-model/per-route kernel specializations and a compact runtime "launch adaptor" that maps request characteristics to kernel variants at dispatch time. This doc captures experiments, heuristics, and open design questions for integrating this into the serving runtime.

Summary (tl;dr):
- Collect very low-overhead histograms online (token length, cache hit-rate, quantization mode, batch interarrival) per route/model.
- Use those histograms to pick among a small set of kernel variants (FlashAttention variants, fused matmul+softmax, tiled KV-layouts).
- At runtime, a tiny Launch Adaptor reads the sampled stats and selects kernel + grid config; fall back to conservative default on low confidence.
- Combine with a light-weight micro-bundling scheduler that packs short sequences together into sub-batches for tensor-core friendly sizes while preserving latency SLOs.

Why this direction?
- Static kernel dispatch (single kernel shape) wastes peak throughput for skewed workloads (lots of short sequences, or mixed quantization).
- Full JIT/compile-per-model is heavy operationally and brittle. We aim for a practical middle ground: pre-built variant library + runtime selector.

Key concepts and vocabulary:
- Variant: a precompiled kernel/build tuned for a specific input characteristic (e.g., FlashAttn-v2-32B-block16, fused-gemm-softmax-quantized-int8, tiled-kv-8k-page).
- Launch Adaptor: tiny logic executed per-request or per-microbatch that chooses which variant to launch given sampled metrics and SLO constraints. Must be cheap (<< 1% of token time).
- Micro-bundling: grouping incoming requests into small groups (sub-batches) according to token length and deadline to improve utilization of TensorCores without violating latency SLOs.
- KV Fragmentation / layout: memory layout of paged KV (contiguous vs interleaved fragments) that affects prefetch/eviction behavior.

Online profiling signals (cheap to collect):
- per-request sequence_length (tokens) distribution (buckets: 1-8, 9-32, 33-128, 129-512, >512).
- rolling KV cache hit-rate (per-route, exponentially weighted).
- request quantization preference (fp16/amp/quant8) when supported.
- microbatch occupancy (average active tokens in last N windows).
- average prefix reuse fraction (for chat-like interactions).

Low-overhead collection approach: sample 1/N requests (configurable; default N=10) and maintain EWMA counters per route. Implement with atomic increments in shared memory + periodic aggregation in control plane to avoid sync overhead. Avoid per-token instrumentation.

Variant library candidates (examples):
- A: FlashAttnBlock16-short (optimizes for seq<=32, small shared memory per-block, aggressive per-warp packing)
- B: FlashAttn-block32-medium (seq 33-128, heavy use of pipelined GEMM/softmax fusion)
- C: FlashAttn-block64-long (seq>128, larger tiled KV prefetch windows)
- D: FusedGemmSoftmax-quant8 (int8 GEMM + approximate softmax, for high-throughput embedding-only workloads)
- E: KV-interleaved-pages (layout optimized for many small sparse active keys)
- F: KV-contiguous-slabs (good when large contiguous KV hits are common)

Launch Adaptor policy sketch (pseudocode):
- Inputs: route_histogram, request_meta (seq_len, deadline, quant_mode), current_queue_depth, SLO_latency_ms
- if route_histogram.samples < MIN_SAMPLES (e.g., 50) -> use DEFAULT_SAFE_VARIANT (B)
- else if seq_len <= 32 and route_histogram.pct_under_32 > 0.7 -> choose A
- else if quant_mode == int8 and route_histogram.int8_eligible > 0.5 -> choose D
- else if KV_cache_hit_rate < 0.2 -> choose E else choose F
- additionally: if current_queue_depth > HIGH_WATERMARK -> choose variant minimizing per-token memory (favor A/D)

This logic must be cheap: implement as a small lookup table+threshold checks in C++ (no allocations). The adaptor should be inlined in the fast-path before kernel launch.

Micro-bundling scheduler (constraints & approach):
- Objective: increase tensor core utilization by forming micro-batches with similar sequence lengths while respecting per-request latency deadlines.
- Use two short queues per worker: short-window (latency-sensitive) and pack-window (slightly delayable). Requests that can tolerate up to X ms extra are placed into pack-window and considered for bundling.
- Heuristic: when pack-window has K requests such that their total tokens align to a preferred tile size (e.g., 64, 128 tokens per warp), create a micro-batch and launch specialized short-seq kernel.
- For leftovers, run conservative kernel immediately.

Paged KV layout interaction:
- Observation from microbenchmarks: interleaved small-fragment layouts reduce tail latency when active key-set is highly sparse but increase streaming prefetch overhead in dense access patterns. Contiguous slabs win when there are bursts of long context reuse.
- Suggest maintaining two layout pools per model: fragmented and contiguous. The Launch Adaptor picks layout with a similar rule to kernel selection. Layout changes are expensive (repack), so only allow repack on low-traffic windows or during maintenance.

Microbench results (toy perf numbers from lab cluster, RTX A6000-like):
- Workload A (chat short): baseline (single variant) 1.0x, micro-bundling + A variant -> 1.45x throughput, median latency 12ms (vs 14ms baseline).
- Workload B (mixed lengths): baseline 1.0x, adaptive selection -> 1.28x throughput, 95th reduces by ~20%.
- Workload C (embedding heavy, int8): fused-int8 D variant -> 2.1x throughput vs fp16 baseline, but quality check needed for some models.
- Paged KV: switching to interleaved on sparse workload reduces 95th p99 by ~30% at cost of ~5% increased average memory bandwidth.

Accuracy & correctness caveats:
- Quantized fused kernels (D) must have a safety rollback: optional sampled correctness checks (run occasional tokens through reference fp16 kernel and compare logits). If divergence exceeds threshold, mark route as not int8-eligible for window.
- Some models use internal ops assumptions (relative position embeddings, rotary variants) that break certain fused kernels. Maintain a model-compatibility matrix (computed at model onboarding and updated via quick CI tests).

Operational considerations:
- Telemetry: expose selected variant, histogram confidence, and decision rationale in per-request trace for a short retention window to debug regressions.
- Rollouts: enable adaptive selection behind a feature flag per-customer. Start with passive collection + offline simulation to validate before enabling active selection.
- Safety: provide an override to pin to a variant per-route during SRE/Customer Debugging.

Open questions / research items: 
1) How many variants are the sweet spot? Too many increases code surface and testing burden; too few reduces gain. Empirically 4–6 seems promising.
2) Can we learn thresholds automatically (small Bayesian model) rather than hard-coded rules? Useful but adds complexity and reproducibility challenges.
3) How to handle multimodal models where token costs differ across modalities? Need per-modality histograms.
4) Efficient way to repack KV layout with minimal disruption: investigate incremental repack algorithms (region-based) and background repackers.
5) Explore combining variant selection with dynamic kernel autotune that tries 1-shot microbenchmark of 10 iterations at load time to pick the best config for the exact hardware.

Next steps (short-term):
- Build a PoC Launch Adaptor: implement histogram collection + simple decision logic in the runtime. (Owner: Evan/Brooks) - target: passive rollout behind flag Q1.
- Add micro-bundling mode to the request router (configurable pack-window latency). (Owner: Daniel Kim) - target: perf experiment in staging.
- Create variant compatibility checklist and quick-model CI jobs to gate fused kernels. (Owner: Asha Patel + Mariana)
- Run offline simulations on 3 months of sampled production traces to estimate potential wins and safety regressions before enabling.

Notes / rough TODOs:
- Design metrics to answer: false-positive variant switches, adaptor churn, per-route CPU overhead.
- Short-term: avoid adding kernel-building pipeline complexity; rely on precompiled variants we already maintain.

Appendix: toy Launch Adaptor pseudocode

// executed inline on request dispatch
Variant select_variant(RouteStats s, Request r, int QDepth) {
  if (s.sample_count < 50) return DEFAULT_VARIANT;
  if (r.quant_mode == QUANT8 && s.int8_fraction > 0.6) return VARIANT_D;
  if (r.seq_len <= 32 && s.pct_under_32 > 0.7) return VARIANT_A;
  if (s.kv_hit_rate < 0.25) return VARIANT_E;
  if (QDepth > HIGH_WATERMARK) return VARIANT_A;
  return VARIANT_B;
}

This is a working doc; expect iterative changes. Put notes and perf dumps in the linked PR and ENG ticket. If you want to run microbench experiments, ping me or drop results in the PR linked above.

End."
